strengths: Novel theoretical framework analyzing regularization in performative learning for realistic repeated risk minimization (RRM) setting; first to characterize how regularization can cancel performative effects

Technically sophisticated analysis with rigorous deterministic equivalent characterization (Theorem 3) for performative fixed points in over-parameterized regime, building carefully on recent high-dimensional statistics tools

Counterintuitive insights including: (1) negative optimal regularization possible, (2) optimal risk improves with performative effects reinforcing trends in over-parameterized regime, (3) optimal regularization direction depends on noise level
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and thorough proofs; explicit formulas for optimal regularization proportional to performative effect strength (Corollary 2, Theorem 4)
Honest discussion of limitations and appropriate restriction to structured setting to enable rigorous analysis
weaknesses: Severely restricted scope with unclear generalizability: linear regression only with Gaussian features, specific coordinate-wise performative model form (y = x^T θ* + x^T D θ + noise), label shifts only—extension to nonlinear/deep models not discussed

Limited experimental validation: only synthetic performative shifts on 2 datasets (Housing 8 features, LSAC 22 features); no real performative shifts, no comparisons to alternative mitigation strategies, no ablation studies

Practical applicability severely limited: requires knowing performative effect b̄ in advance (contradicting main motivation), requires covariance structure Σ and Schur complement S₁, no implementation guidance, complex formulas unsuitable for practitioners

Over-parameterized analysis restricted to small ρ (weak spurious correlations) and specific block-diagonal covariance structure; effects of spurious feature performativity hidden by ρ² factor suggesting limited relevance; only analyzes 2 iterations rather than true fixed point

Testing on untouched distribution D(θ=0) is theoretically clean but doesn't reflect real deployment where performance matters on D(θ*) where θ* is new equilibrium; evaluation choice limits practical relevance
No ablation studies on sensitivity to assumption violations; missing analysis of when regularization should NOT be used; no empirical comparison to estimation-based methods despite criticizing them
Deterministic equivalent technique relies heavily on Han & Xu (2023) and Ildiz et al. (2025) without introducing substantial new methodological innovation

strengths: Novel perspective on handling performative effects through principled regularization scaling rather than difficult effect estimation, with minimal computational overhead

Rigorous theoretical analysis with elegant characterizations: closed-form optimal regularization in population regime (Corollary 2) and precise deterministic equivalent in over-parameterized regime (Theorem 3)

Interesting non-obvious phenomenology: performativity can improve optimal risk in over-parameterized regime when reinforcing existing trends (Theorem 4, Equation 26); noise level determines regularization behavior (Equation 24)
Well-presented problem formulation (Assumption 1) and careful mathematical development progressing logically from population to over-parameterized regimes
Empirical validation across multiple datasets and regimes shows theoretical predictions are reasonably robust despite violations of stated assumptions (non-Gaussian data, nonlinear relationships)
Comprehensive appendix with complete proofs and extension to higher-order approximations
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: optimal regularization depends on unknown performative effect b, yet practitioners cannot know b in advance. Claim of 'setting regularization in anticipation' lacks concrete guidance

Highly restrictive modeling assumptions limit generality: linear regression only, label shifts (features remain centered), diagonal D structure, ||b||∞, ||c||∞ < 1, artificial assumption that spurious features have zero true coefficient
Artificial evaluation metric: testing on D(θ=0) rather than the deployment distribution D(θ_∞) that practitioners actually face. Justification about 'bias amplification' is weak
Weak treatment of spurious features: effects of c negligible in first-order approximation and O(ρ²) in second-order. In practice, spurious features are major concern in performative settings

Limited scope of over-parameterized analysis: only 2 iterations to approximate fixed point; specific covariance structure Σ=[Id ρId; ρId Id]; small parameter approximations (ρ, b̄, c̄) of unclear quality in realistic regimes

Weak experimental validation: (i) synthetic performative effects don't validate model assumptions; (ii) no baselines or comparison to existing performative learning methods; (iii) no experiments on failure cases or model violations
Limited practical utility in population regime: optimal risk always worse than non-performative baseline, so main benefit limited to special case of over-parameterized reinforcing effects

Missing guidance on key practical questions: robustness to covariance misspecification, performance with nonlinear effects, selection of performative features, behavior with longer deployment horizons

strengths: Novel application of high-dimensional statistics to performative learning; first systematic characterization of optimal regularization scaling with performative effect strength
Rigorous mathematical framework with non-asymptotic concentration bounds (Theorem 5.1) and detailed proofs; extensions to sub-Gaussian data show robustness

Interesting theoretical phenomenology: optimal regularization direction depends on noise level (Eq. 21-22), and optimally-regularized risk can improve when performativity reinforces existing trends (Eq. 24)
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation, comprehensive related work, and good use of figures to illustrate theory; thoughtful impact statement addressing fairness considerations
Results generalize beyond ridge regularization to dropout, Lasso, and elastic net; preliminary validation on neural networks suggests broader applicability
Provides actionable guidance: optimal regularization λ* scales proportionally with performative effect strength b̄, enabling practitioners to anticipate effect
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical model (linear regression, label shifts only, diagonal D, specific block covariance) is restrictive; real data has complex covariance (Figures 9a-9b) and deep learning is fundamentally nonlinear

Empirical validation limited to 2 small real datasets (8 and 22 features) with synthetic performative shifts added—doesn't validate that actual performative effects follow the assumed label-shift model; neural network experiment (Figure 5) is qualitative illustration only without theoretical guarantees

Over-parameterized analysis (Theorem 5.1) only covers exactly 2 iterations with approximation error O(‖D‖²_op); unclear how small ‖D‖_op must be for approximation to be useful; high-probability bounds Cpe^{-pδ⁴/C} lack tightness analysis

Testing on untouched distribution D(θ=0) rather than deployment distribution D(θ_∞) creates mismatch between optimization objective and actual use case; fairness justification is stated but practical applicability is uncertain

Practical utility requires estimating/knowing performative parameters b̄, c̄ and effect structure; Theorem 5.2 results depend on functions B₁(σ,κ) that depend on unknown quantities, creating gap between theory and actionable guidance

Restrictive model of performativity: label shifts only (no feature shifts), diagonal D matrix, linear dependence on θ; real strategic behavior may be more complex; limited to ridge regularization in main theory
